## What the problem is

R users routinely write a procedure that works on one case (one file,
one region, one subject, one parameter set) and then need to run it on
many. The step from "a script that works once" to "a run over a hundred
cases" is usually improvised: a `for` loop or `lapply()` with an ad hoc
`tryCatch()`, some `future` code added for speed, and no record of
which package versions were loaded or which input files were read. When one case fails, the run often stops, or the
failure goes unnoticed. When an upstream file is rewritten between two
runs, nothing flags it. When someone asks what exactly was run, the
answer is reconstructed from memory.

## Who it affects

Anyone who applies the same procedure to many entities. The primary
setting, and the proposer's own practice, is file processing in public
statistics and recurring reporting: the same processing applied to
every region, or every month over the same paths, where the run must
be auditable (which code, which inputs, which cases failed and why) and
a silently modified input file is a common cause of a wrong number
reaching a decision maker. The same pattern appears in clinical data
pipelines (one derivation per study or site, with traceback and
environment capture required for review) and in simulation studies
(thousands of parameter sets, where one failure must not cost the
others).

## Why it should be solved

Each team pays the same improvisation cost on its own, and the code it
produces is rarely reusable or auditable by anyone else. Error handling
in `apply()`-style loops is a frequent user question (see Consulted).
Codifying the pattern once, behind a stable contract, lowers that cost
for the whole community, as `testthat` did for testing. The aim is a
proposed, versioned contract for iterated runs in R, with `genproc` as
its reference implementation.

## Existing work

Every ingredient exists. `purrr` [@purrr] gives `safely()` and
`insistently()` (retries); `furrr` [@furrr] and `future.apply`
[@future; @future.apply] map in parallel on `future`; `progressr`
[@progressr] signals progress. `BiocParallel` [@BiocParallel] flags
failed elements (`bpok()`), re-runs only those (`BPREDO`) and logs
tracebacks. `batchtools` [@batchtools] keeps a job registry that can be
inspected and resumed. `targets` [@targets] branches over rows and
files, saves workspaces for debugging, and manages a whole project's
dependencies; `genproc` is designed to run inside a target, not instead
of one.

What none of them offers for a standalone batch procedure is one call
on a function and a table that returns, in one object, the per-case log
with tracebacks, the environment and input-file snapshot, and the means
to re-run only what failed or changed, with no job registry to set up
and no pipeline to restructure. `genproc` [@genproc] returns that
object today. It targets procedures that write their output per case
(a file, a table, a database row); collecting in-memory return values
is out of scope. Whether this interface saves implementation and
recovery work is the claim that Milestone 4 tests with outside users.
What is missing today: the written contract behind the mask, the
layers that make failed cases replayable and long runs observable,
evidence from users other than the author, and the stewardship that
lets the package outlive him.
